estranged: He is brushing a horse. You come into the stable and he does not stop and does not turn round. The rhythm of the brush does not change.
He lifts his eyes to you for a moment, then bends to check a shoe. There was no hostility in the look. It only confirmed something he already knew.
cold: “Mm.” He leans the hayfork against the wall and waits for you to speak. When you have finished he is still standing there, as though waiting for something more useful.
He nods and goes back to what is in his hands. You stand behind him a while and he does not look up again.
neutral: He stops, turns round, waits. There is not one unnecessary part in any of it.
accepted: “It will rain this afternoon,” he says, and only then looks at you. “If you are going out, not the west road.”
He comes out from the back of the stable with oil still on his hands. “The grey is not right today. Take another if you are riding.”
trusted: He moves half a step over and leaves the wooden crate clear. This is how he invites you to sit.
“That thing you said last time.” He says it while he is untying a rein, with nothing in front of it. “I have thought about it.”
embraced: When you come into the stable your horse is already saddled and the tack is on the hook nearest your hand. He is busy with something at the other end and does not turn round.
“Morning.” He does not say that word twice in a day.

estranged: “Morning,” she says, and her eyes do not leave the board. The two others in the kitchen go quiet at the same moment without arranging it.
She puts the lid on the soup pot, more gently than usual. “What are your orders, sir.” She used the word orders.
cold: “Well now, Steward.” The voice is bright and the smile is the standard one. “Was there something?” Her hands never stop.
“You have come at just the right moment,” she says, and turns away to reach something down off a shelf, without saying right for what.
neutral: “Steward, come in, come in, do not stand in the doorway, that is where the draught is.” She pulls out a stool, and then wipes it again.
“I was only just wondering when you would come by.” She laughs loudly. She has said that to everyone who ever arrived here.
accepted: “You have come at the right moment. May I say it straight out?” She sets down the rolling pin and wipes both hands on her apron.
“The household on the west side has asked again.” Straight to it, the greeting left out altogether.
trusted: “Hold this for me.” Without looking up, she pushes the handle end of the pot over towards you.
“Sit.” She points at the far end of the table. “I have put water on. You do not look well.”
embraced: There is a small dish set out on the table. It is the thing you happened to say last week that you liked. She says nothing about it and goes on with her onions.
“There is some in the pot,” she says. “Without the thing in it. The thing you do not eat.”

estranged: She is wiping the stair rail. Seeing you come down, she puts the cloth into the bucket, turns side-on out of the way, and waits for you to pass.
“Sir.” Her head is down, and two steps later she is at the other end of the corridor.
cold: “Sir.” She stops what she is doing, waits until you have finished, and nods. Through all of it her eyes rest on the window behind you.
She shifts the folded sheets to her other arm and puts the free hand to the door. “Is there anything you need.” She does not say it as a question.
neutral: “Good morning, sir.” Her voice is very quiet, and her head goes down as soon as it is said. Her hands do not stop for long.
“Upstairs is done,” she says, and then pauses, as though there were half a sentence more. She does not say it.
accepted: “I shut the windows; there was a wind in the night.” She pauses. “The table in your room, the leg is a little loose. I will have someone look at it.”
“Good morning, sir.” She does not go straight off after saying it. She turns the cloth round in her hand and wipes again over a place she has already wiped.
trusted: “Mr Gregor did not eat his breakfast today,” she says. What she notices is always of this kind.
“Sir.” She stops, and waits for you to speak first. She would not have waited before. She would have found a reason to go.
embraced: “Morning,” she says. No sir. And having said it she stays where she is, as though this were also a place she is allowed to stand.
She is wiping the windows, and seeing you come in she lays the cloth over the rim of the bucket and turns round. She used to turn side-on out of the way.

estranged: “May the hearth-fire keep you.” A slight bow of the head. It is the line kept for strangers.
He is feeding the hearth, and only turns round when he has finished. “Steward. Was there something you wanted to ask?”
cold: “The season turns quickly.” Then he looks at the fire and does not go on.
“You have caught me badly; I was about to go.” He has no intention of going. He does not sit down either.
neutral: “Steward. Sit a while? The fire has only just come up.”
“This estate’s forge-chapel is well set,” he says. “Light in the morning, none in the afternoon. Whoever laid it out understood the work.”
accepted: “You have been here some days now.” He puts another piece of wood on the fire. “How are you settling?”
“There is something I have been meaning to ask you.” He says it slowly. “There is no hurry. You need not answer.”
trusted: “Why do you stay?” He asks it straight out, and adds at once: “I am not asking you to answer now.”
“Metal is at its quietest while it is tempering.” He moves the coals about. “So are people. You have been very quiet lately.”
embraced: He shifts over and motions for you to sit. For a long time he says nothing at all, and only watches the fire.
